en.marketHeading: What is actually different about marketing in {city}
market: {city} has a large institutional employment base. Provincial government, health care and post-secondary education anchor the city, which makes local employment steadier than {region}'s reputation suggests and makes the consumer economy more predictable than in a purely resource-driven town. If you sell to households here, that stability is worth something: the demand does not fall off a cliff the way it can elsewhere in the province.

The private side is heavily weighted toward {industries}. Those businesses have a demand curve that is driven by weather and shutdown schedules rather than by anything a marketer does. Roofing, concrete, landscaping, HVAC and paving in {city} live or die on a short window, and the single most common mistake I see is a budget divided evenly across the year. Spending the same amount in February as in June is not fairness, it is a transfer to whoever bid properly in June.

The third thing is geography. A meaningful share of the region's population and industrial activity sits outside the city in {nearby}, and the industrial corridor northeast of the city is where a lot of the money is. Targeting the City of {city} alone leaves out customers who consider themselves local.

en.servicesIntro: Same three services everywhere I work. What changes in {city} is timing more than mix: for a lot of businesses here the question is not how much to spend but when, and getting that wrong wastes more money than any targeting mistake.

services.title: Google Ads Management
services.body: Strong fit for {city} trades and home services, where the customer has an urgent problem and picks somebody that week. The work is account structure, conversion tracking that counts booked jobs rather than form views, and a budget schedule that loads your season instead of spreading flat across a year when half of it produces nothing.

services.title: SEO Consulting
services.body: The channel that fixes the other half of the seasonality problem, because rankings you earn in the slow months are working for you when the season arrives. Technical fixes first, then pages that answer what {city} buyers actually search, including the surrounding communities you serve.

faq.q: Do you have an office in {city}?
faq.a: No. I am based in Toronto and work from home, so there is no {city} office and I am not going to imply there is. Everything is run remotely over video and email, which is how I run every account regardless of city.

faq.q: Our business is seasonal. Should we advertise year round?
faq.a: Usually not at the same level, no. For most seasonal {city} businesses I would concentrate the ad budget in and just ahead of the season, keep a small presence through the slow months so you are not restarting from zero, and use the quiet period to build the SEO that will be ranking by the time demand returns. Flat monthly budgets are the most common waste I find in seasonal accounts.

faq.q: Which service should an {city} business start with?
faq.a: If your season is close and you need the phone ringing, Google Ads. If you are in a slow stretch with a few months before demand picks up, that is the best possible time to start SEO, because the work needs time and you have it. AIO is the cheapest to add and the one your {city} competitors are least likely to have started.

faq.q: Do you work with businesses in Sherwood Park and St. Albert?
faq.a: Yes, and with the rest of the region. Everything is remote, so the municipality makes no difference to the work or the price. If anything, businesses in the surrounding communities are often the ones with the most obvious targeting gaps to fix.
Google Ads management is $1,500 a month plus your ad spend. SEO consulting is $1,200 a month. AIO consulting is $1,800 one time. No setup fees and no long contract.
